mcqs.question: Why does the on-the-fly-vs-precompute decision for derivatives matter especially for an image hosting service?
options: Because precomputing even a handful of common sizes per image multiplies total stored bytes by roughly that many sizes, at billions-of-images scale
Because images cannot be resized after they are uploaded
Because storage cost is irrelevant once images are uploaded
Because every image is only ever requested at its original size
mcqs.explanation: At huge catalog scale, precomputing even 4 common sizes per image multiplies stored derivative bytes roughly 4x beyond the originals — a real cost that has to be weighed against on-the-fly generation. Images can absolutely be resized post-upload; storage cost very much matters at this scale; and images are typically requested at many different sizes, not just the original.

mcqs.question: What's the typical production approach for serving images at multiple sizes?
options: Store the original only and never generate derivatives
Precompute every conceivable size for every image regardless of demand
Precompute the handful of sizes almost every image needs, and fall back to cached on-the-fly generation for uncommon sizes
Resize on every single request, even for the most commonly requested sizes
mcqs.explanation: A hybrid approach precomputes the few sizes nearly every image is requested at (cheap upfront, fast to serve) while handling rare sizes on demand and caching the result — balancing storage cost against latency. Storing only the original pushes all latency onto every request; precomputing every possible size wastes storage on sizes nobody asks for; and resizing every request even for common sizes wastes compute repeatedly.

mcqs.question: A redesign introduces a new thumbnail size, and thousands of images on the updated page are requested at that size simultaneously. What prevents this from overloading the resize workers?
options: Refusing to serve any image until every possible size has been precomputed in advance
Rolling back the redesign automatically whenever a new size is detected
Deleting the original images to force a smaller catalog
Request collapsing — simultaneous requests for the same image at the same new size share one resize job instead of each triggering its own
mcqs.explanation: Collapsing simultaneous identical resize requests into one job is what prevents a thundering-herd spike on the resize workers. Requiring every size precomputed upfront defeats the point of on-the-fly generation; auto-rollback and deleting originals aren't real mitigations and would break the product.

mcqs.question: Why does hashing an uploaded image's filename fail as a deduplication strategy?
options: Filenames are cryptographically impossible to hash
Filenames are arbitrary and can coincidentally collide or differ regardless of the actual image content, so filename hashing misses true duplicates and can falsely match different images
File systems don't allow files with the same name to exist
Deduplication is unnecessary for image hosting services at any scale
mcqs.explanation: The real problem is that filenames carry no information about content — coincidental matches ('image.jpg') falsely dedup different photos, and identical photos uploaded with different names never get deduped at all. Filenames can be hashed trivially, so that's not the issue; storage systems handle same-named files fine; and dedup matters a great deal at billions-of-images scale.
